experiments.question: Do context management (H1), hang protection (H2) or typed report digests (H9) cut tokens, cost or wall time without losing hidden-test passes?
experiments.result: H1 lowered cost by 32.8 percent (interval -53.3 to -4.3) but tokens by 65.6 percent with an interval that includes zero (to +0.9), so it met the rule on one reading and not the other. Its wall time fell 18.1 percent but the interval includes zero once the blocks with a run stopped by the time limit are left out. H2 lowered cost by 1.5 percent (interval -31.4 to 12.6): no difference detectable. H9 lowered cost by 16.1 percent, below the bar. 5 of 12 blocks passed the hidden tests in the baseline and 5 in H1; two of the 4 tasks were passed by no arm.
experiments.setup: 4 tasks, 3 repeats, four arms (the baseline A0 and H1, H2, H9), 48 valid runs of 51, the low-cost model gpt-6-luna, stopping after stage 2 (no Vivado). Each task and repeat is a block with all four arms in rotated order. Pre-registered adopt rule: a primary metric at least 30 percent better with an interval that excludes zero, and no loss of tests passed.

experiments.decision: The gate was merged into the flow and replaces reliance on the tool's report alone.

experiments.lesson: Where the standard tool is silent, a small deterministic check can be decisive. Seed the fault yourself and show which check sees it.

experiments.question: Does a gate that checks the structure of the asynchronous paths and simulates with injected synchroniser delay catch clock-crossing faults that the tool's own CDC report does not?
experiments.result: The tool's CDC report alone flagged 5 of the 10 faulty designs. The new gate flagged 10 of 10, with 0 false alarms on the 12 correct designs. The table was identical on the re-measurement on Vivado 2026.1.

experiments.decision: The exceptions gate is part of the build flow. A later fix stopped it failing every build with a debug core, whose own ignored exceptions it had counted as the design's.
experiments.interval: Fixtures, one run each. The drills show the gate's logic; they say nothing about how often real designs have such exceptions.
experiments.lesson: A gate that fails every build is as broken as one that passes every build. Test it on a clean design and on a faulty one.

experiments.result: The gate's verdict matched the expected verdict on 14 of 14 drills, of which 10 were expected to be flagged. A further row of the 15 is an alternative design with no exception and no expected verdict.
experiments.setup: 15 drill designs on Vivado 2026.1, each with an exception that is either correct or harmful (too broad, a typo that matches nothing, a false path over a binary bus), re-timed without the exception and after routing.
experiments.title: Do timing exceptions hide failures, and can a gate see them?

experiments.decision: The loop stays as a repair tool with its limits stated. The plan's comparison on other designs is not run.
experiments.interval: None: one run per case, so these are illustrations, not rates. Two builds of the same unchanged RTL differed by about 0.05 ns of slack.
experiments.lesson: An early with-plan run accepted a design whose core had been removed by synthesis; Icarus allowed two blocks driving the same registers and Vivado tied them to ground. That run is not counted, and it is why a synthesis guard exists. A passing simulation is not a passing build.

prs.title: Brief 62A: closure loop, timing playbook, report digests and design-time timing plan

experiments.question: Can a loop that edits the RTL, re-checks it on an independent bench and rebuilds close a timing miss, and does a design-time plan help?
experiments.result: c13_hough_lines closed in one iteration, from -0.225 to 0.61 ns of worst slack without the plan. Of 3 seeded misses, 1 closed; c14_int8_dot_requant stopped at the 5-iteration limit at -5.27 ns (from -24.601) and c11_nco_mixer at -1.569 ns (from -4.401). When the RTL was written with the plan, none of 6 attempts passed the hidden bench, so no first build with the plan exists.
experiments.setup: Vivado 2026.1, xc7a100tcsg324-1, whole-board builds. The RTL writer was gpt-6-luna. One run per case: c13_hough_lines with and without the plan, and 3 seeded misses made by raising a task's clock. The hidden bench is always the acceptance check.
experiments.title: Can the agent repair a timing miss by itself?

experiments.decision: The build cache is part of the flow. Threads stay at one under the memory cap, since results are identical and the gain was small.
experiments.interval: Two runs per thread count, other jobs shared the PC that night, so wall times carry that load. The no-cache time is modelled from the measured fresh-build stages.
experiments.lesson: Check the result is identical before you celebrate a speed-up. Several figures from the earlier release were withdrawn because they could not be repeated under the new memory cap.

prs.title: Brief 33: faster Vivado runs (build cache, thread count, cloud burst runner)

experiments.question: Does the thread count change results or time, and can a cache and resumed builds cut an agent run's build time without changing the result?
experiments.result: Placement and routing hashes and slack were identical at every thread count. The mid-size design c13 took 546 s at one thread and 413 s at four; the small design c10 showed no measurable gain. The cache cut one agent run's build sequence by 76 percent on c10 and 80 percent on c13, with identical hashes and slack.
experiments.setup: Fresh builds of three designs on Vivado 2026.1, one at a time under a 6 GB memory cap, at one, two and four threads, and one agent run's build sequence replayed with and without the cache.
experiments.title: Do more threads or a build cache make Vivado runs faster?

findings.finding: Spec items were lost silently, the reference model and the RTL disagreed on an interface, and stale test files stayed in the build.
findings.fix: A schema so no spec item is lost, one model contract with a check, and superseded tests deleted.

findings.finding: The RTL writer used a stage's whole budget so the Verifier never got a turn.
findings.fix: A turn reserve per role, and files kept across repair visits.

findings.finding: A live run set its own V3 thresholds low in its own plan and passed.
findings.fix: Fixed floors in a file the agent never writes, and a minimum number of evaluated mutants.

findings.finding: The agent invented a register map that only the hidden spec held, and never asked for it.
findings.fix: The Clarifier must ask for a map that is not given, and the oracle answers with the whole map.

findings.finding: A top-level port was named LED0 where the board constraints and the bench use the bus LED.
findings.fix: Rule FDA-CON-7: a port must be a master-constraints name or a bus of one.

findings.finding: The simulate summary showed a follow-on error and hid the first exception.
findings.fix: The first exception is put at the head, and test files are import-checked before pytest starts.

findings.finding: The assertion checkers were not in the Verilator builds, so cover properties read as zero.
findings.fix: Checkers are added to every Verilator build, and stage 2 gets more visits.

findings.finding: The Claude Code CLI updated itself and the arm refused the untested version.
findings.fix: The accepted version list was updated after a live tool-text check; later evaluations pin the binary.

findings.finding: A hidden bench read a high-impedance value from a legal design (a pull-up the simulator drops on a variable port), and a spec left a weight encoding unstated.
findings.fix: The bench resolves the pull for both port styles, the spec states the encoding, and a pin scan covers every bench.

findings.finding: Scoped XPM constraints were not applied, so a clock crossing showed negative slack with no exception.
findings.fix: A script applies them after synthesis, and a probe design records the effect.

findings.finding: Skipped and expected-fail tests were counted as passing tests.
findings.fix: The gate counts them as not passing.

findings.finding: A timed-out build left Vivado running.
findings.fix: The runner gets its own process group and kills it.

findings.finding: A call that loaded several skills overflowed the output limit and silently cut the middle out of each.
findings.fix: Whole skills are returned up to the limit, and those held back are named.

findings.finding: The exceptions gate failed every build with a debug core, whose own ignored exceptions it counted as the design's.
findings.fix: Those are information, and the design's own still fail.

findings.finding: A test run moved the checkout it ran from.
findings.fix: A session guard compares branch and head, and git variables are scrubbed from child processes.

findings.finding: A benchmark reference design missed timing on Vivado 2026.1.
findings.fix: Two pipeline stages were added under a dated amendment, with the acceptance tests and mutants unchanged.

findings.finding: A closure run accepted a design whose core synthesis had removed.
findings.fix: A synthesis guard, and the run was marked invalid and not counted.

findings.finding: Independent review found claims in agent-written handovers that the records did not support.
findings.fix: The DOC step's request and checks were tightened, and the handovers regenerated.

findings.finding: Three adversarial reviews each defeated the regular-expression source scan of the reset check.
findings.fix: Replaced by elaboration, failing closed, with a regression set and attack designs.

lessons.claim: The agent's own checks are not a pass.
lessons.evidence: 6 of 21 development runs passed their own checks and failed the hidden tests, each from a spec read differently.

lessons.claim: Where the standard tool is silent, a deterministic gate can see the fault.
lessons.evidence: The tool's own CDC report alone flagged 5 of 10 faulty designs; the gate flagged 10, with 0 false alarms on 12 correct designs.

lessons.claim: A test bench that looks complete can miss reset-state faults.
lessons.evidence: The first full mutation run killed 90.48 percent of 21 mutants; the survivors were both reset-state faults.

lessons.claim: A cheaper model is not evidence of equal quality.
lessons.evidence: Paired over 86 problems, one cheaper model was 12.4 points worse (interval -21.7 to -3.5) and the other showed no detectable difference.

lessons.claim: A tool the roles do not use cannot be measured.
lessons.evidence: With the router on, end-to-end hidden passes were 0 and with it off 0; the roles hardly called the new tools.

lessons.claim: Few blocks show only large effects, and a rule needs one reading.
lessons.evidence: H1 lowered cost by 32.8 percent (interval -53.3 to -4.3) and tokens by 65.6 percent (interval to +0.9), so the adopt rule gave two answers.

lessons.claim: One run per case is an illustration, not a rate.
lessons.evidence: 1 of 3 seeded timing misses closed, and none of 6 attempts to write RTL with the design-time plan passed its hidden bench.

lessons.claim: Pin every tool that is not under test.

method.text: A task's tests are written from its spec and never shown to the agent. Passing means the hidden tests pass, the code-run gates pass and, for hardware tasks, the board agrees. The agent's own testbench never counts, and no language model ever produces a score.
method.title: Hidden tests decide

method.text: The agent is stochastic, so every task runs several times (3 in the first evaluation) and two versions of the agent are compared on the same tasks, with an interval, not two means. With 19 tasks a pass rate was planned to be known to about plus or minus 17.5 points, which shows a large difference and not a small one.
method.title: Repeats and pairs

method.text: Development tasks are for finding and fixing faults. Held-out tasks decide, are touched rarely, and a fix is never derived from them. Where one was seen, as in eval-1, it moves to development.
method.title: Development and held-out

method.text: Knowledge comes from documentation, never from the benchmark. A leak guard fails the site build if text from private tasks appears, and during scored runs the agent searches only a frozen library.
method.title: Nothing leaks

method.text: Before a scored run the arms, tasks, repeats, comparisons and stopping rules are written down and committed. The CLI, model and tool versions are pinned and recorded with every run.
method.title: Pre-register, then pin

method.text: A measurement changes one thing at a time. When several changes ship together, nothing is attributed to any of them. A correctness bug in the measuring instrument is the exception, and is fixed on one case.
method.title: Change one thing

method.text: An evaluation is retired when it is saturated, no longer measures what is wanted, is contaminated, is not comparable after a change to the tools, or is too noisy. It becomes a regression suite. eval-1 was retired by a scope decision before it produced a score.
method.title: Retire, do not delete

text.best: Best result: a deterministic CDC gate flagged 10 of 10 faulty designs where the tool's own report flagged 5, with 0 false alarms on 12 correct designs. Not proven: how often the agent solves a task it has never seen. The first held-out evaluation was stopped with no score, and the baseline evaluation has not been run.
text.fine_tune: A fine-tuning experiment on a narrow sub-problem (choosing a closure strategy when timing is tight) is planned and has not been run. It will be added here as one more card, whatever it finds, including a no.
text.glossary: Terms used below: CVDP is a public set of RTL-writing problems. CDC is a signal crossing between two clocks. A mutant is a design with one deliberate fault, used to test whether the tests notice. An escape is a run whose own checks passed while the hidden tests failed. Slack is how much timing margin a path has; negative means it fails. V0 to V3 are the four verification stages. H1, H2 and H9 are three harness changes (context management, hang protection, report digests). Slack and WNS both mean timing margin. An oracle answers the agent's clarifying questions from the hidden spec. ILA is an on-chip logic analyser. MCP is the protocol the agent's tools speak. Stage 2 is the RTL and tests stage. The Clarifier, Modeller, Verifier and Designer are the agent's four roles. The models are named as the provider lists them.
text.lede: How the FPGA Design Agent was designed, measured and corrected. The agent turns a plain-English request into a design checked by hidden tests, code-run gates and a board. This page shows how that was built and tested, one experiment at a time, including the ones that found nothing.
text.limits: The grouping of the timeline and the cause class of each finding are the author's reading of the pull request text, not a measurement. The findings listed are the ones with a recorded fix, not a complete count of the agent's faults. Most experiments ran one model on a small task set, and each card says so. Results measured on an earlier Vivado release and not repeated on Vivado 2026.1 are not shown. The list of merged pull requests is a snapshot from the day the page was built.
text.scope: 11 experiments are written up below, each in the same form. Where a run was single or the sample small, the card says so and claims no rate.
